safety.text: Follow the age label; knobs and pieces must be firmly attached and too big to fit in the mouth.
Keep the toddler's puzzle pieces out of a baby's reach, and watch what gets handed to the baby.

why.text: HSE lists simple puzzles for 1–2-year-olds as good for hand–eye coordination and problem-solving; CDC suggests naming each piece as it goes in.

activities.title: Feed the teddy
activities.summary: Give your toddler a teddy or doll, a spoon, a cup and a cloth, and take turns pretending to feed it and tuck it in.

notes: Younger toddlers often copy one action; longer pretend stories tend to come later.

supervision.space: Floor space anywhere in the room; pretend food only, no real food or drinks.

steps: Sit on the floor with teddy, a spoon, a cup and a cloth.
Show one pretend action, 'Teddy's hungry. Yum!', as you spoon pretend food to teddy.
Hand over the spoon and take turns; follow their ideas, like a drink, a nap or a bump to kiss better.
adaptations: Younger toddler: just one action, a drink from the cup, and lots of copying.
Older toddler: add a second toy and a little story: teddy's bath or teddy's walk.
Talk through the toy: let teddy ask your toddler a question.
stopCues: Asking for real food: a snack cue, not part of the game

safety.text: Pretend food only, with big unbreakable toy dishes; nothing small enough to fit in the mouth.

why.text: AAP says pretend play lets young children try out social roles and builds communication and language; CDC suggests pretend-feeding a stuffed animal and taking turns.

activities.title: Find the hidden toy
activities.summary: Hide a favorite toy with a bit still showing, ask 'Where's teddy?' and give hints until your toddler finds it.

items: A cushion, cloth or box to hide it under

supervision.space: One child-proofed room; hide things at floor level, never on shelves or furniture they'd climb.

steps: Let your toddler watch you hide a favorite toy under a cushion or cloth, with a bit sticking out.
Ask 'Where's teddy?' and wait; point or give a hint if they need it.
Celebrate the find, then hide it again somewhere new at floor level.
adaptations: Younger toddler: hide it under one cloth right in front of them.
Older toddler: hide it fully out of sight, or hide yourself behind a chair.
Two children: an older sibling does the hiding while you cheer.
stopCues: Upset when they can't find it

safety.text: Hide things at floor level only, and anchor furniture; searching toddlers climb.

why.text: AAP suggests hidden-toy hunts for 12–18-month-olds and describes hide-and-find games as practice with the idea that things still exist out of sight.

activities.title: Sock basket helper
activities.summary: While you sort clean laundry, hand your toddler socks to drop into a basket, then let them push or carry it, thanking them for helping.

supervision.space: Wherever you fold laundry, away from the iron, detergent and laundry pods.

steps: Sit on the floor with the clean laundry and a basket between you.
Hand over socks one at a time, 'Sock in!', and let them drop or throw them into the basket.
Say thank you, then let them push or carry the basket a short way to a drawer.
adaptations: Younger toddler: in and out of the basket, as many times as they like.
Older toddler: find the matching sock, or make a pile of all the little ones.
Tidy-up version: toys into a box at the end of play, with a clean-up song.
stopCues: Pulling the folded pile apart (a cue to stop, not to scold)

safety.text: Keep detergent, laundry pods and the iron out of sight and reach while your toddler helps.

why.text: CDC suggests letting toddlers help with everyday tasks, such as putting socks or toys in a basket, and praising them for helping.

activities.title: Toddler-led walk
activities.summary: Walk a safe route at your toddler's pace and let them lead, stopping to squat, look and collect a few big leaves.

notes: New walkers manage short stretches; bring a stroller or carrier for the rest.

items: Optional: stroller or carrier for the way home
Optional: a paper bag for leaves

supervision.space: Sidewalks, paths or a park away from traffic; hold hands near roads, driveways and crossings.

steps: Pick a short, safe route on sidewalks, paths or in a park, and bring the stroller for the way back.
Let your toddler set the pace and choose the stops: cracks, bugs, puddles, leaves.
Hold hands near any road, driveway or crossing; let go only on paths away from traffic.
Collect a few big leaves in a bag and keep an eye on what goes into hands and mouths.
adaptations: New walker: walk a few minutes, ride a while, walk again.
Older toddler: copy animals you see, running like a squirrel or flapping like a bird.
Baby too: the baby rides in the stroller or carrier while the toddler walks holding your hand.
stopCues: Tired legs or asking to be carried
Darting toward the road: time to hold hands or ride

safety.text: Hold your toddler's hand near traffic and at crossings; stick to sidewalks or paths and stay off driveways.
Check hands and mouths often: no berries, mushrooms or small stones. Collect big leaves only.
Dress for the weather; in sun use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.
Let them out to walk: WHO advises not keeping young children strapped in a stroller for more than an hour at a time.

why.text: AAP suggests child-led walks, saying toddlers practice walking, running, squatting and climbing as they explore; ZERO TO THREE suggests collecting leaves.

activities.title: Toddler area at the playground
activities.summary: Visit a playground's toddler area and stay within arm's reach as your toddler tries low steps, ramps, small slides and bucket swings.

notes: Look for posted age signs; equipment for older children isn't sized for toddlers.

supervision.space: Toddler-sized equipment over soft surfacing; you within arm's reach whenever they're off the ground.

steps: Head for the toddler section: low climbers, ramps, small slides, spring rockers and bucket swings.
Check the ground is soft (mulch, sand or rubber), slides aren't hot, and nothing is tied to the equipment.
Stay within arm's reach on anything off the ground; spot them up the steps and at the slide's end.
Mix in running on the grass and a sit-down break in the shade.
adaptations: New walker: ramps, low steps and the bucket swing, with you in front.
Confident climber: a low ladder and small slide, still with you right there.
Busy playground: go at a quieter time or stay in the fenced toddler area away from running older kids.

safety.text: Use toddler-sized equipment and stay within arm's reach; toddlers need closer supervision than older children.
Touch slides and metal before use; they can burn in the sun. No hood drawstrings, helmets or cords around the neck.
Use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin; avoid the hottest hours.

why.text: CPSC lists low climbers, ramps, small slides, spring rockers and full-bucket swings as toddler equipment; AAP says outdoor play helps build balance.

activities.title: Scoop-and-pour water tub
activities.summary: Sit right beside your toddler at a shallow basin of water with cups, spoons and a funnel; tip the water out the moment you finish.

items: Plastic cups, spoons and a funnel

supervision.space: You within arm's reach the whole time, phone away; towel under the basin; water emptied right after.

steps: Put a shallow basin with just a little water on a towel, indoors or outside.
Sit right beside your toddler, phone away, and hand over cups, spoons and a funnel.
Pour together and name what happens: full, empty, splash, drip.
When you finish, tip the water out straight away and put the basin out of reach.
adaptations: Younger toddler: one cup and one spoon; splashing and grabbing is the game.
Older toddler: add a sponge to squeeze or toys that float and sink.
Baby at home too: do this while the baby sleeps or another adult has them.
stopCues: Putting their face in or drinking the water
Tipping the basin or throwing water

safety.text: Stay within arm's reach with full attention the whole time; toddlers can drown in an inch or two of water.
Empty the basin as soon as play ends; never leave water standing, and an older child can't be the one watching.
Wipe up spills; wet floors are slippery. Outdoors, add shade and a hat.

why.text: HSE lists jugs and a basin for water play for 1–2-year-olds as sensory play that builds hand–eye coordination; CDC and ZERO TO THREE suggest cups, spoons and a funnel.

activities.title: Over, under, in and out
activities.summary: Set up a cushion to crawl over, a table to crawl under and a laundry basket to climb in and out of, saying each word as they go.

items: Sturdy table or chair to crawl under

supervision.space: Floor level only, away from stairs and hard edges; table and shelves stable or anchored.

steps: Lay out a floor cushion, then a sturdy table to crawl under, then an empty laundry basket.
Show the way, saying each word: 'Over the cushion... under the table... in the basket... out!'
Stay within arm's reach at the basket, where wobbles are most likely, and go round again.
adaptations: Cautious mover: start with just the cushion and the basket, with you on the far side.
Walking toddler: step over the cushion and walk around the table instead of under it.
Add 'through' with a big cardboard box opened at both ends as a tunnel.
stopCues: Bumping their head under the table

safety.text: Keep everything at floor level, with cushions on the floor and never stacked on sofas, and spot within arm's reach.
Use a sturdy table and anchored furniture; climbing toddlers can pull furniture over.

why.text: ZERO TO THREE describes this over-under-in-out game for 12–24 months and says games like it help toddlers learn word meanings while being active.

activities.title: Pretend cook with real pots
activities.summary: Set out a pot, wooden spoons and empty boxes so your child can 'cook' you a pretend meal while you work nearby as the hungry customer.

items: A pot or two with lids

supervision.space: Floor or low table in view, outside the cooking area and away from knives and hot drinks.

steps: Put a pot, wooden spoons, plastic bowls and a few empty food boxes on the floor or a low table where you can see them.
Order a meal from where you're working: 'One soup, please!' Pretend to taste it and ask what's in it.
Let them lead the story: stirring, serving teddy, washing up. Place a new order if play fizzles.
adaptations: Younger: one pot, one spoon, and a teddy to feed.
Older: take turns being cook and customer, or 'write' a menu together.
Baby nearby: give the baby their own wooden spoon and bowl beside the 'kitchen'.
stopCues: Wandering toward the real stove or oven
Losing interest after a few orders

safety.text: If you're cooking, set this up outside the cooking area where you can see them; hot pans and drinks stay out of reach.
Use only unbreakable items too big to fit in the mouth: no dried pasta, beans or bottle caps.

why.text: AAP describes pretend play as a way young children try out social roles and build language; CDC suggests letting toddlers pretend to cook with safe kitchen items.

activities.title: Big box car or house
activities.summary: Turn a large cardboard box into a car or little house, and let your child climb in, decorate it with crayons and play.

items: Optional: a paper plate steering wheel

supervision.space: Clear floor in view; staples and tape removed; box away from stairs, windows and furniture to climb.

steps: Pull out staples and loose tape, cut a door or windows if you like, and stand the box on a clear floor where you can see it.
Ask, 'Is it a car or a house?' and let your child climb in and decide.
Offer chunky crayons to draw wheels, windows or a door, then do your task nearby, checking in often.
adaptations: Younger: leave it plain and play peek-in-the-window from outside.
Older: add a cushion seat and a cardboard-tube 'key', and take a pretend trip together.
Two children: one box each, or one drives while the other rides.
stopCues: Trying to stand on or climb over the box walls
Tearing the box apart in frustration

safety.text: Remove staples and tape first, and keep the box away from stairs, windows and furniture they could climb from it.
Keep crayons out of mouths, and out of a baby's reach if one is nearby.

why.text: CDC suggests turning a big box into a car or house for a 2½-year-old to decorate; AAP describes pretend play as practice with social roles and language.

activities.title: Playdough squish and roll
activities.summary: Sit at the table with store-bought dough and squish, poke, pinch and roll balls and snakes together.

notes: Wait until your child no longer puts dough or craft bits in their mouth.

items: Store-bought dough labeled for your child's age
A rolling pin or a plastic cup to roll with

supervision.space: Seated at a table; dough stays on the table and out of a baby's reach.

steps: Sit together at the table with a lump of store-bought dough each.
Show squish, poke, pinch and roll; make a ball, then a long snake, and name what you're doing.
Add a rolling pin or big cutters and make 'cookies' or a snake family.
Put the lids back on tightly and store the dough up and out of reach.
adaptations: Just starting: squish and poke only; you roll the shapes.
Older: make a face, a pretend birthday cake, or count the balls you've rolled.
Wheat or gluten allergy: check the label; most dough contains wheat.

safety.text: Use store-bought dough labeled for your child's age, not homemade raw-flour dough. Keep it out of mouths and store it out of reach.
Most dough contains wheat; check the label if your child has a wheat or gluten allergy.
Dough bits can choke a baby: keep dough on the table, away from a baby sibling, and check the floor afterward.

why.text: CDC suggests squishing, pressing, pinching and rolling playdough at about 3 to build hand and finger muscles; HSE says playdough helps hands develop strength and control.

activities.title: Paint with water outside
activities.summary: Give your child a small cup of water and a big brush to 'paint' a fence, wall or paving, then watch the marks dry and vanish.

items: A small plastic cup of water
A large paintbrush or a sponge

supervision.space: Yard, patio or path away from the street and driveway; you within arm's reach of the water.

steps: Pour a little water, just enough to dip a brush, into a small plastic cup.
Show how to dip and paint a fence, wall or paving slab; paint big lines and wiggles together.
Watch a mark dry: 'Where did it go?' Paint it again, fast or slow.
Tip the water out as soon as you finish.
adaptations: Younger: use a sponge and dab big splotches.
Older: paint around their shadow, or paint shapes and letters you name.
Hot day: paint in the shade and compare how fast marks dry in sun and shade.
stopCues: Wandering toward the street or driveway

safety.text: Stay within arm's reach with full attention near any water, even a small cup, and tip it out as soon as you're done.
Choose a spot away from the street and driveway.
In sun, use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.

why.text: CDC suggests simple art with 2- and 3-year-olds, and HSE describes water play with jugs and a basin as sensory play that builds hand–eye coordination.

activities.title: Chalk drawing outside
activities.summary: Draw big lines, circles and pictures with chunky chalk on a patio, path or playground, taking turns copying each other.

supervision.space: Patio, yard, path or playground away from the street and driveways.

steps: Pick a patio, path or playground spot away from the street and driveway.
Draw a big line or circle and say 'Your turn!' Copy each other's marks.
Trace around a hand or shoe, add a sun or a road for toy cars, and name the colors.
adaptations: Younger: scribble side by side while you name the colors.
Older: draw a path of circles to jump along, or a face with feelings.
Rainy day: draw with chalk on dark paper at the table.
stopCues: Drifting toward the street or driveway

safety.text: Draw away from the street and driveways; young children shouldn't play where cars go.
Keep chalk out of mouths, and keep broken bits away from a baby sibling.
In sun, use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.

why.text: CDC suggests drawing with crayons or chalk at about 30 months, showing a straight line and then a circle; HSE lists drawing among fine-motor play.

activities.title: Follow-the-leader parade
activities.summary: March around the room or yard in a line, stomping, tiptoeing, turning and stepping backward, then let your child be the leader.

items: Optional: a pot and wooden spoon for a drum

supervision.space: A clear path with no toys, slippery rugs or sharp-edged furniture; away from stairs.

steps: Clear a path and say 'Follow me!' March in a line around the room or yard.
Change the move every few steps: stomp, tiptoe, giant steps, turn around, walk backward slowly.
Swap: your child leads and you copy everything they do.
If you have the energy, add a drumbeat on a pot or a marching song.
adaptations: Younger: hold hands and stick to stomping and tiptoeing.
Nearly 3: add hopping, or freeze whenever the drum stops.
Low energy: sit and call out the moves as they march past you.

safety.text: Clear toys and slippery rugs from the path, stay away from stairs, and walk backward slowly on a flat floor.

why.text: CDC suggests follow the leader with 2½-year-olds (straight lines, turns, backward steps and tiptoeing), then letting the child lead.

activities.title: Floor-level obstacle course
activities.summary: Make a short loop: walk a tape line, step over cushions, crawl under a table and jump a rolled towel, then go round again.

notes: Jumping with both feet is optional; step over the towel until they're ready.

items: A sturdy table to crawl under

supervision.space: Everything at floor level: no climbing on furniture; sharp corners cleared; away from stairs and windows.

steps: Lay out a short loop: a tape line to walk, cushions to step over, a table to crawl under, a rolled towel to jump.
Show each station once, slowly, then let your child try while you stay within arm's reach.
Cheer each lap; change the order or add 'crawl like a bear' when they want more.
adaptations: Younger: step over the towel instead of jumping, and hold a hand along the tape line.
Older: let them choose the order, or carry a teddy through the course.
Small space: just the tape line and the table tunnel.
stopCues: Climbing onto furniture or stacking cushions to climb
Getting wild or bumping into things

safety.text: Keep every station at floor level; no climbing onto sofas, tables or stacked cushions. Children this age don't yet judge danger.
Move sharp-edged furniture out of the way, and make sure nearby furniture and TVs are anchored.

why.text: HSE lists obstacle courses among physical play that builds muscles, bones and movement skills; WHO advises plenty of varied activity through the day for 1–4-year-olds.

activities.title: Color sort into bowls
activities.summary: Put two or three colored bowls on the table and let your child sort big toys and household things by color while you work nearby.

items: Big items in the same colors: blocks, cups, lids, socks

supervision.space: Table or floor in view; every item too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube.

steps: Put two or three bowls out with a pile of big items in matching colors.
Sort one together: 'Red block goes in the red bowl.' Then let them carry on.
Do your task nearby and check in: 'What's in the blue bowl?'
adaptations: Younger: two colors only, or just match socks into pairs.
Nearly 3: sort by size or by kind (cups, lids, blocks), then count each bowl.
Book version: find all the red things on a page of a picture book.

safety.text: Use only items too big to fit through a toilet-paper tube, with no loose or broken parts.
If a baby is nearby, keep the sorting on the table and out of the baby's reach.

why.text: CDC suggests naming colors and, around 3, finding matching objects around the house; AAP says simple objects like containers and blocks help 1–3-year-olds understand how things work.

activities.title: Carry-to-the-table helper
activities.summary: Before a meal, let your child carry napkins, unbreakable cups and spoons to the table, one trip at a time.

supervision.space: Hand items over away from the stove; set the table before any hot food or drinks come out.

steps: Before the food is ready, hand over napkins first, then unbreakable cups and spoons, a few at a time.
Ask them to put one at each place: 'One for Grandma, one for you.'
Thank them for the exact job: 'You gave everyone a spoon!'
adaptations: Younger: carry napkins only, one at a time.
Nearly 3: count the places together first.
After the meal: carry the cups back to the counter.
stopCues: Losing interest: thank them and finish yourself

safety.text: Keep it to cool, unbreakable items. Hot dishes, drinks and knives stay with you, and your child stays out of the cooking area.

why.text: CDC suggests letting 2-year-olds help get ready for meals, such as carrying cups or napkins to the table, and thanking them for helping.

activities.title: Wipe-the-table helper
activities.summary: After a meal or snack, give your child a damp cloth to wipe the table while you tidy up nearby.

items: A damp cloth or sponge (water only)

supervision.space: Table cleared of food, plates and hot drinks; cleaning sprays put away out of reach.

steps: Clear plates, food and hot drinks first, then hand over a damp cloth with water only.
Show one big wipe, then let them wipe in circles or 'drive' the cloth around the table.
Carry on tidying nearby and admire the shiny table together.
adaptations: Younger: wipe their own high-chair tray or one small patch.
Older: wipe the chairs too, then drop the cloth in the laundry basket.
Short on time: one wipe each, then a high five.
stopCues: Climbing onto the table or chair
Bored: thank them and take over

safety.text: Plain water only. Keep cleaning sprays and detergents capped and stored out of sight and reach.
Wipe from the floor or while sitting on a chair; no climbing onto the table.

why.text: CDC suggests letting toddlers help with simple everyday tasks and thanking them for helping.

activities.title: Who, what, where? Book chat
activities.summary: Share a picture book and pause on each page to ask a simple who, what or where question, letting your child point or answer.

items: A picture book with clear pictures

supervision.space: Side by side on the sofa, floor or bed.

steps: Let your child pick the book, even if it's the same one again.
On each page, ask one easy question: 'Who's that?' 'What's he eating?' 'Where's the cat?'
Wait for a point or a word, then add a little more: 'Yes, the cat is under the bed!'
adaptations: Younger: name the pictures and let them point.
Nearly 3: before you turn the page, ask 'What will happen next?'
Tired: just look at the pictures together; you don't have to read every word.
stopCues: Wriggling away or closing the book

safety.text: Choose sturdy books for a child who still chews or tears pages, and pick up torn bits.

why.text: CDC suggests reading with 2½-year-olds and asking simple who, what and where questions, then around 3 asking what will happen next.

activities.title: Library story time
activities.summary: Go to a story or rhyme time at your local library, then let your child choose a book or two to borrow.

notes: Check your library's schedule; session times and ages vary.

items: Stroller for the trip, if needed

supervision.space: Sit together during the session; keep your child beside you near doors, stairs and the parking lot.

steps: Check the library's story or rhyme time schedule and pick a session that misses nap time.
Sit with your child, join the songs and actions, and let them watch first if they're shy.
Afterward, let them choose one or two books to borrow, and read one at home later.
adaptations: Shy or new: sit near the back and leave whenever you need to.
No session today: visit the children's section and read one book there.
Baby too: hold the baby on your lap while your toddler sits beside you.
stopCues: Overwhelmed by the group: step out for a break

safety.text: Hold hands in the parking lot and near roads on the way; young children need an adult with them near traffic.
Keep your child beside you near stairs and exits.

why.text: CDC suggests reading together and visiting the library, and visiting libraries or parks with other children to practice sharing and taking turns.

activities.title: Playground: the 2-to-5 area
activities.summary: Visit a playground area made for ages 2 to 5 and let your child climb low steps, ramps and small slides while you stay close.

notes: Many playgrounds post an age sign; choose equipment marked for 2–5.

supervision.space: Equipment sized for ages 2–5 over soft surfacing; within arm's reach whenever they climb or are off the ground.

steps: Find the area or sign for ages 2–5 and check: soft ground underneath, nothing broken, no ropes tied on, slides not hot.
Let your child choose: ramps, low steps and ladders, small slides, spring riders.
Stay within arm's reach while they climb, and let them slide down on their own, not on your lap.
Leave time to run on the grass, and give a five-minute warning before you go.
adaptations: Newer climber: stick to ramps and stairs, holding a hand on the steps.
More confident: try a low ladder, or a belt or bucket swing with you pushing gently.
Busy playground: find a quieter corner or come back at a calmer time.

safety.text: Check for soft surfacing, broken parts, ropes tied to equipment and hot slides; remove drawstrings, scarves and helmets.
Don't go down a slide with your child on your lap; their leg can catch and break.
Stay within arm's reach on climbing equipment; young children don't yet judge heights or danger.
In sun, choose shade and use a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.

why.text: AAP says playgrounds let children exercise their bodies, brains and social skills; CPSC lists ramps, low ladders, small slides and spring rockers as suited to ages 2–5.

activities.title: Nature find walk
activities.summary: On a short walk or park path, look for a few things together (something red, a big leaf, a bird, a puddle) and let your child lead.

notes: Short legs tire quickly; bring the stroller for the way home.

items: Optional: a paper bag for big leaves

supervision.space: Paths or a park away from traffic; hold hands near roads, driveways and parking lots.

steps: Before you go, pick three or four things to find: something red, a big leaf, a bird, a dog, a puddle.
Walk a safe route at your child's pace and let them lead the hunt; cheer each find.
Hold hands near any road, driveway or parking lot.
Collect big leaves only; look at berries, mushrooms and small stones but leave them where they are.
adaptations: Younger: one thing to find, like 'a dog!', and name everything else you pass.
Older: find something soft, rough, round and tall, or count the birds.
Baby too: the baby rides in the stroller while your toddler walks holding your hand.
stopCues: Tired legs or asking to be carried
Darting toward the road: hold hands or ride

safety.text: Hold your child's hand near traffic, driveways and parking lots; young children need an adult with them near roads.
Check hands and mouths: no berries, mushrooms or small stones. Collect big leaves only.
Dress for the weather; in sun use shade, a hat and sunscreen on exposed skin.

why.text: CDC suggests letting a 3-year-old choose and lead play in a park or on a trail; AAP says child-led walks let toddlers practice walking, running, squatting and climbing.

activities.title: Big-sticker picture
activities.summary: At the table, let your child peel big stickers, press them onto paper, and draw around them with chunky crayons.

notes: For children who no longer put small things in their mouth.

supervision.space: At a table in view; stickers, backing scraps and crayons kept out of a baby's reach.

steps: Lift the edge of each sticker a little to get them started.
Let them stick, peel and re-stick on the paper; offer a theme like 'stars in the sky' or 'animals on a walk'.
Add crayon roads, grass or clouds, then do your task nearby and check in.
adaptations: Just starting: you peel, they press.
Older: make a sticker story and tell it to you.
Another day: decorate a big box house with the stickers.
stopCues: Sticking them on walls, furniture or a sibling

safety.text: Stickers and backing bits can choke a child who still mouths things; gather scraps afterward and keep them away from a baby.
Keep crayons out of mouths while drawing.

why.text: CDC suggests letting a 2½-year-old decorate with crayons, paint or stickers; HSE lists drawing among fine-motor play.

activities.title: Sit-down snack together
activities.summary: Sit down together at a table, bench or picnic blanket for a small snack, and chat about what you've just done.

notes: Offer foods your child already eats safely; ask their clinician about allergies or feeding concerns.

items: A snack your child already eats, cut small

supervision.space: Child seated at a table, in a high chair, or on a bench or blanket; you within arm's reach, screens off.

steps: Wash hands, then sit your child at the table, in a high chair, or on a bench or blanket.
Offer a small portion of a food they already eat, cut into small pieces, with a drink of water.
Sit with them and chat about the morning: 'What did you climb at the park?'
Snack stays seated: if they get up to play, the food stays at the table.
adaptations: After the playground: sit on a bench together before heading home.
Younger: buckled into a high chair, with very small, soft pieces.
Older: let them choose between two snacks and carry cups to the table.
stopCues: Standing up, running or lying down with food in their mouth

safety.text: Seated eating only, with you right there: no walking, running, playing or lying down with food in the mouth. Cut food small; encourage chewing.
Until about 4, skip high-risk choking foods: hot dogs, nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, raw carrot sticks, apple chunks, hard candy, chunks of meat or cheese.
Know your child's food allergies and follow any allergy plan; watch what older children hand to a baby.
Screens off during snacks and meals.

activities.title: One calm show while you cook
activities.summary: While you make dinner, put on one calm, slow-paced episode made for preschoolers, with your child in view and away from the stove.

notes: Optional. A toy, activity or small job near you (outside the cooking area) works too.

supervision.space: Child on the sofa or floor in your view, outside the cooking area; screen on a low, stable stand or anchored.

steps: Choose one calm, slow-paced episode made for preschoolers, such as Mister Rogers' Neighborhood (its producer lists it for ages 2–4).
Turn off autoplay so it stops after one episode, and settle your child where you can see them, away from the stove.
Cook, glance over often and answer when they call; switch the screen off when the episode ends.
At dinner, screens off. Ask one question about the show: 'Who did you see? What happened?'
adaptations: No screen today: a toy, puzzle or small job near you, outside the cooking area.
Want to join in: watch the last few minutes together and talk about it.
Upset or overtired: comfort first; AAP and HSE advise against using a screen to calm a child down.
stopCues: Asking for another: offer a helper job instead
Over-excited or upset by the show

safety.text: A show doesn't replace supervision: keep your child in view and out of the cooking area, with hot pans and drinks out of reach.
Put the TV or tablet on a low, stable stand or anchor it; TVs can tip onto climbing children.

why.text: HSE recognizes screens can feel easier while cooking; UK and Irish guidance favor calm, slow-paced shows, and AAP suggests quality content with autoplay off.

activities.title: Watch one together and talk
activities.summary: Sit together for one short, calm episode, pause now and then to talk about it, and afterward do one thing from the show.

supervision.space: Side by side on the sofa or floor; screen on a low, stable stand or anchored.

steps: Pick one calm episode made for your child's age, and turn off autoplay.
Sit together. Pause once or twice to name what's happening or how someone feels: 'She looks sad. Why?'
When it ends, switch off and do one thing from the show: sing its song, draw it, or act it out.
adaptations: New to screens: a shorter episode, or a video call with family instead.
Older: let them retell the story or choose what to act out.
Low energy: watch together and ask just one question at the end.
stopCues: Scared or upset by something in it
Begging for more: move straight to the follow-up activity

safety.text: Put the TV or tablet on a low, stable stand or anchor it; TVs can tip onto climbing children.
Keep screens off at meals and in the hour before bed.

why.text: AAP suggests watching alongside your child and talking about shows or doing something related; Canadian and Irish guidance also advise watching together.

activities.title: Copycat moves: hop, tiptoe, march
activities.summary: Take turns being the leader: tiptoe, march, hop and jump while the other copies.

notes: Hopping and skipping come at different times for different children; marching and tiptoeing work for everyone.

supervision.space: Clear, non-slip floor or yard; away from stairs, sharp table corners and the street.

steps: Say 'Copy me!' and tiptoe across the room, then march with high knees.
Add hops, jumps, giant steps and tiny mouse steps, naming each move as you do it.
Swap so your child leads and you copy. Trade leader every minute or so.
Finish slowly: stretch tall, curl up small, tiptoe to the sofa.
adaptations: Not jumping yet: march, stomp, tiptoe and turn in circles instead.
Older: hop on one foot, skip, or string three moves together to copy in order.
Tired parent: sit and call out moves while your child does them.
stopCues: Getting wild or bumping into things
Out of breath or flopping down
Frustrated with a move: switch to an easier one

safety.text: Play on a clear floor away from stairs and furniture they might climb; children this age fall off anything they can climb.

why.text: HSE suggests copycat moves like tiptoeing, skipping, jumping and hopping for 3- to 5-year-olds; AAP suggests silly walks where children take turns as leader.

activities.title: Red light, green light
activities.summary: Call 'green light' to go and 'red light' to freeze as your child moves toward you, then swap roles.

supervision.space: A long clear room, hallway, yard or park lawn, well away from the street and driveways.

steps: Stand at one end of the space; your child starts at the other.
'Green light' means walk or run toward you; 'red light' means freeze like a statue.
Mix it up: 'yellow light' for slow motion, or 'tiptoe light' and 'hopping light'.
When they reach you, swap so your child calls the lights and you move.
adaptations: Younger: walking only, and hold up something red or green as you say it.
Older: freeze in a pose you name, or play Simon Says moves at each green light.
Small room: freeze dance to music instead.
stopCues: Upset about being caught moving: drop the 'go back' rule
Running too fast to stop safely

safety.text: Play away from the street and driveways. If something rolls toward the road, an adult fetches it.

why.text: CDC suggests red light, green light or freeze dance to help 4-year-olds practise stopping and waiting when they are excited.

activities.title: Throw, catch and kick a big ball
activities.summary: Take turns throwing, catching and kicking a big soft ball, stepping back a little as it gets easier.

notes: Catching takes lots of practice; many children trap the ball against their chest at first.

items: Optional: a laundry basket or box as a target

supervision.space: Fenced yard, park lawn or open room away from the street, windows and breakables.

steps: Stand a few steps apart. Bounce the big ball to your child and say 'hands ready!'
Take turns: they throw to you, you bounce it back. Step back a little after a few catches.
Kick it back and forth, then try kicking or throwing it into a basket or box.
Count catches together and cheer the tries as much as the catches.
adaptations: Easier: roll the ball, or use a bigger, softer ball caught against the chest.
Harder: a smaller soft ball, overhand throws, or a plastic bat and a big ball.
Indoors: soft ball only, thrown into a laundry basket.
stopCues: Frustrated after missed catches: go back to rolling
Ball play turning into throwing at people or windows

safety.text: Teach them never to chase a ball into the street; an adult fetches it.

why.text: HSE suggests more kicking, catching and throwing at this age, and CDC suggests balls and plastic bats for preschool play.

activities.title: Trike or balance-bike ride on a path
activities.summary: Helmet on, then let your child ride a trike, balance bike or scooter on a park path while you walk alongside.

notes: Ready when they can get on, steer and stop with their feet. AAP says many children are ready for a trike around 3.

items: Bike helmet with a safety-standard label

supervision.space: Park paths or a closed play area, never the street or driveway. Stay within arm's reach near any road.

steps: Helmet on and buckled snug, closed-toe shoes on, every ride.
Walk to a path or park away from cars, holding hands and wheeling the trike across roads.
Walk alongside while they ride. Practise stopping when you say 'stop!' at each corner or bench.
Head home before legs get tired; carrying a trike and a tired child is hard work.
adaptations: Not pedaling yet: push along with feet on a balance bike or ride-on.
More confident: ride a loop of landmarks, stopping at each one.
Scooter: helmet on too; start with both feet, then push off with one.
stopCues: Tired legs or falling more often
Not stopping when asked: time to walk it home
Too hot, too cold, or getting dark

safety.text: A snug, safety-certified bike helmet on every ride, plus closed-toe shoes; ride only on paths or in closed areas, away from streets, driveways and pools.
Children this age don't understand traffic. Hold hands at every crossing and never let them ride in the street or a driveway.
Helmet off before climbing on playground equipment; the straps can catch.
Dress for the weather; in sun, use shade, a hat or sunscreen.

why.text: HSE suggests trikes, balance bikes and scooters for 3- to 5-year-olds, and NHS lists scooting and riding a bike as active play for under-5s.

activities.title: Playground: climb, slide and swing
activities.summary: Head to a playground with preschool-sized equipment and let your child choose, spotting them on climbers.

notes: Choose equipment that suits your child's size and confidence, not just their age.

supervision.space: Equipment sized for ages 2–5 over soft surfacing; within arm's reach on climbers and ladders.

steps: Pick equipment made for preschoolers. Check the ground is soft and slides aren't hot.
Let your child choose. Stay within arm's reach on climbers, ladders and high platforms.
Practise swing pumping: lean back with legs out, then lean forward with legs tucked.
Slides go feet first, one at a time; walk well clear of moving swings.
adaptations: Cautious child: low climbers and the small slide first, holding your hand on steps.
Confident child: monkey bars with you spotting, or a climb-slide-run circuit.
Short on time: a 15-minute run-around still gives a good active break.
stopCues: Tired, clumsy or taking bigger risks
Upset over turns: take a break on a bench

safety.text: Check for soft surfacing (not concrete or grass), hot slides and sharp edges; no drawstrings or bike helmets while climbing.
Stay close on climbing equipment: falls from play equipment are a common injury at this age.
On sunny days use shade, a hat and sunscreen, and bring water.

why.text: CDC suggests playground visits where 5-year-olds learn to pump a swing and try monkey bars; AAP says playgrounds exercise bodies, brains and social skills.

activities.title: Nature hunt: find and count
activities.summary: Name five things to find outside, such as a leaf, a stick and something yellow, and count the finds together.

items: A paper bag or egg carton for finds

supervision.space: Park, yard or quiet paths. Hold hands near roads and driveways.

steps: Draw or say five things to find: a leaf, a stick, a smooth stone, something yellow, something soft.
Walk slowly and let your child spot them. Count each find together as it goes in the bag.
Look for 'same and different': two matching leaves, a big stone and a small one.
At the end, lay the finds in a row and count again. Leave flowers, bugs and nests where they are.
adaptations: Younger: three big, easy things to find.
Older: find ten of one thing, or one thing for each color you name.
Rainy day: hunt for colors and shapes from a window or doorway.
stopCues: Tired legs or asking to be carried

safety.text: Hold hands near roads, driveways and crossings, and stick to paths and sidewalks.
Look, don't taste: no berries, mushrooms or leaves in mouths, and stay off freshly sprayed lawns. Wash hands afterward.
Dress for the weather; in sun, use shade, a hat or sunscreen.

why.text: AAP suggests preschoolers collect twigs, leaves, cones and rocks outdoors, and CDC suggests counting everyday things you see.

activities.title: Big and small opposites game
activities.summary: Crouch low for 'small', stretch up for 'big', then act out fast and slow, and loud and quiet, together.

supervision.space: A clear patch of floor with nothing sharp to bump into.

steps: Crouch down low and say 'I am small!' Then stretch up tall: 'I am big!'
Your child copies. Try fast and slow walking, loud and quiet voices, high and low hands.
Call out one word, such as 'slow!', and let them show you the opposite.
Let them pick an opposite for you to act out.
adaptations: Younger: stick to big and small, and loud and quiet, doing them together.
Older: add up and down, open and closed, happy and sad faces, in and out of a box.
Low energy: sit and play it with hands, faces and voices only.
stopCues: Too silly to listen: finish with a slow, quiet round

safety.text: Keep the fast moves to a clear floor, away from stairs and furniture they might climb.

why.text: CDC suggests an opposites game for 3-year-olds: small and big, fast and slow, quiet and loud.

activities.title: Picture book: what happens next?
activities.summary: Read a picture book and pause to ask what is happening and what will happen next, then let your child retell it.

items: A picture book with a story

supervision.space: Anywhere you can sit side by side and both see the pictures.

steps: Sit together with a story that has clear pictures.
Before turning a page, ask: 'What do you think will happen next?'
Ask about a picture, 'What's happening here? How does she feel?', and ask for one more detail.
At the end, let your child tell the story back while turning the pages.
adaptations: Younger or tired: one question every few pages; pointing counts as an answer.
Older: invent a new ending together, or act the story out with toys.
Very tired parent: lie down and let your child 'read' you a book they know.
stopCues: Wants the story without questions: just read it

safety.text: If a baby joins in, give them a board book of their own and keep small story props out of their reach.

why.text: CDC suggests asking preschoolers what is happening in the pictures and what will happen next; WHO encourages reading and storytelling with a caregiver.

activities.title: Take-turns made-up story
activities.summary: Start a story with one line, let your child add the next bit, and keep taking turns until it ends.

supervision.space: Anywhere you can hear each other: the sofa, a waiting room, bedtime.

steps: Start with one line: 'Once there was a dog who lost his…'
Your child adds what happens next. Then you add a bit, and keep taking turns.
Help with questions: 'Who came along? What did they do? Then what?'
End it together, give it a title, and retell it later at dinner.
adaptations: Younger: you tell most of it and they add a word, a name or an animal sound.
Older: use 'first, next, finally', or put your child in the story.
Stuck for ideas: start from a toy, a picture or something you can see.
stopCues: Upset about where the story is going: let them steer

safety.text: It's talk only. If you play it in the car, the driver keeps their eyes on the road.

why.text: WHO encourages storytelling with a caregiver during sitting time, and AAP lists telling stories among skills many 3- to 5-year-olds are building.

activities.title: I spy: colors, shapes and sounds
activities.summary: Say 'I spy something red' and let your child hunt for it, with clues; then they spy and you guess.

supervision.space: Anywhere you can both look around: the kitchen, a waiting room, the park.

steps: Look around and say 'I spy something red!' Your child hunts and points.
Give clues if needed: 'It's round… it's on the table.'
Try sounds ('I hear something that beeps') or shapes ('something square').
Swap so your child spies and you guess.
adaptations: Younger: colors only, with the thing in plain view.
Older: first sounds ('something that starts with b') or two clues at once.
Hot and cold: hide a toy and say 'warmer' or 'colder' as they search.
stopCues: Frustrated after several wrong guesses: give a big hint
Bored: switch to a moving game

safety.text: Keep guesses to things they can see or reach from the floor, with no climbing to touch the answer.

why.text: CDC suggests games like I Spy, card games and Hot and Cold to help with memory and attention around age 5.

activities.title: Matching pairs memory game
activities.summary: Lay picture cards face down and take turns flipping two at a time to find matching pairs.

items: A matching or memory card game
Or homemade pairs drawn twice on scrap card

supervision.space: A table or patch of floor big enough to lay the cards out in rows.

steps: Start with 4–6 pairs face up and find the matches together: 'Same or different?'
Turn them face down in rows. Take turns flipping two cards.
If they match, keep them. If not, turn them back over and say what you saw.
Add more pairs as it gets easy; stop while it's still fun.
adaptations: Younger: play face up as a 'find the same' game.
Older: more pairs, or picture lotto with boards to fill.
No game at home: draw simple pictures twice on scrap card.
stopCues: Upset about losing: play as a team instead
Too many cards: take some away

safety.text: If a baby is around, keep cards and any small game pieces out of their reach.

why.text: CDC suggests matching games at 3 and 4 and card games at 5; HSE lists lotto games for 3- to 5-year-olds.

activities.title: Sock matching and laundry sort
activities.summary: Tip clean socks on the floor for your child to pair up and sort by person or color while you work nearby.

items: A pile of clean, dry socks

supervision.space: On the floor in view of you, away from the washer, dryer and laundry products.

steps: Tip clean socks onto the floor and ask your child to find the pairs.
Sort into piles: yours, mine, the baby's, or by color.
When you check in, count the pairs together.
Let them carry each pile to the right room.
adaptations: Younger: two piles, big socks and little socks.
Older: fold small towels in half, or match and count ten pairs.
Odd sock left over? Make it a mystery to solve later.
stopCues: Socks become a throwing game: fine, or call it done

safety.text: Keep detergent, pods and other laundry products locked away, out of sight and reach.

why.text: CDC suggests letting preschoolers help with simple chores and lists matching socks among jobs many 5-year-olds do.

activities.title: Draw, then tell me about it
activities.summary: Set out paper and crayons at the table where you can see them; later ask your child to tell you about the picture.

supervision.space: A table in view of you; caps and crayons kept away from any baby or younger sibling.

steps: Set out paper and crayons or washable markers at a table you can see.
Let them draw whatever they like while you get on with something nearby.
Check in: 'Tell me about your picture.' Ask why and how, and write their words on it.
Caps back on and crayons gathered up when they're done.
adaptations: Younger: big paper taped to the table and chunky crayons.
Older: draw lines and shapes together, a person, or the letters of their name.
Keep an 'activity box' of paper and crayons they can fetch themselves.
stopCues: Drawing on the table or walls

safety.text: Marker caps and broken crayon bits can choke a baby or toddler: keep them out of younger siblings' reach.

why.text: CDC suggests an activity box of paper and crayons, drawing together, and asking 'why' and 'how' about what a child makes.

activities.title: Jigsaw puzzle at the table
activities.summary: Give your child a jigsaw labeled for their age to work on at the table while you're nearby, checking in now and then.

items: A jigsaw puzzle labeled for their age
Optional: a tray to keep pieces together

supervision.space: A table or floor in view of you, out of any baby's reach.

steps: Pick a puzzle labeled for their age and tip the pieces onto a tray, picture side up.
Show them how to find corners and straight edges first, then step back.
Check in now and then: 'What color goes next to the sky?'
Count the pieces back into the box so none are left on the floor.
adaptations: Easier: fewer, bigger pieces, or a frame puzzle.
Harder: more pieces, or a big floor puzzle.
First time: build it together, then let them do it alone.
stopCues: Frustrated: help with a piece or two

safety.text: Puzzle pieces can be small. Keep them away from babies and younger siblings, follow the box's age label, and check the floor afterward.

why.text: CDC suggests toys that get children putting things together, such as puzzles; WHO lists puzzles among good sitting-time activities with a caregiver.

activities.title: Playdough squish, roll and cut
activities.summary: Set out playdough on a tray for squishing, pinching and rolling, with a rolling pin and cutters, while you're nearby.

items: Blunt plastic knife or cookie cutters

supervision.space: A table or tray in view of you; dough and small tools away from any baby or younger sibling.

steps: Put the dough on a tray or placemat at a table you can see from where you're working.
Show squishing, pinching and rolling balls and snakes, then leave them to it.
Add a rolling pin and cutters for shapes; count the shapes when you check in.
Squash it all back into the tub with the lid on so it doesn't dry out.
adaptations: Easier: hands only, for squashing, poking and pulling.
Harder: make letters, a pretend meal or a dough person.
Give two colors and see what happens when they mix.

safety.text: Keep dough crumbs and small cutters away from babies and younger siblings, and check the floor afterward.
Most playdough contains wheat. If anyone has a wheat allergy, check the label; reactions can follow touch as well as eating.

why.text: CDC suggests squishing, pressing, pinching and rolling playdough, saying it builds the hand and finger muscles later used for writing, buttoning and cutting.

activities.title: Snip paper strips with child scissors
activities.summary: Sit beside your child and help them snip strips of scrap paper with child-safe scissors, then glue the snips into a picture.

notes: If cutting is hard, tearing paper is a fine start.

items: Strips of scrap paper or junk mail

supervision.space: Seated at a table with you beside them. Scissors stay at the table and away from any younger child.

steps: Cut scrap paper into strips about two fingers wide.
Show the grip: thumb in the top hole, fingers below. Open and close like a crocodile mouth.
Hold the strip for them at first while they snip it into little pieces.
Glue the snips onto paper to make a picture, then put the scissors away.
adaptations: Not ready for scissors: tear paper into pieces instead.
Older: cut along a drawn straight line, then a wavy one.
Left-handed child: left-handed child scissors may be easier.
stopCues: Cutting hair, clothes or anything else: scissors away

safety.text: Use only child-safe scissors. Store kitchen and adult scissors and knives separately, out of reach.
Cut sitting down, and put the scissors away before you turn to a baby or another job.

why.text: AAP lists using child-safe scissors among hand skills many 3- to 4-year-olds are building, and CDC suggests child scissors in a preschool art box.

activities.title: Wash the fruit and veg
activities.summary: On a sturdy step stool at the sink, your child scrubs and rinses firm fruit and vegetables in a bowl of cool water.

notes: Needs to stand steadily on a step stool, with you right beside them.

items: A bowl of cool water or a colander

supervision.space: At the sink on a sturdy stool with you beside them. Cool water only; stove off or well out of reach.

steps: Set a sturdy step stool at the sink and run cool water into a bowl.
Hand over firm fruit or vegetables; they rub each one with their hands and rinse it.
Count them into a colander and pat dry with a towel.
Empty the bowl as soon as you've finished.
adaptations: Younger: wash plastic cups and spoons instead.
Older: scrub potatoes with a clean vegetable brush.
No room at the sink: a bowl of water on a low table, with you right there.
stopCues: Climbing or leaning too far over the sink

safety.text: Stay right beside them with full attention while there's water, and empty the bowl when you're done.
Use a sturdy, non-slip stool and stay within arm's reach while they stand on it.
Cool water only, and keep them away from the stove and the hot tap.
This is a washing job, not a snack: raw carrot sticks and apple chunks are choking risks for under-4s.

why.text: CDC suggests giving 3-year-olds simple meal jobs, such as washing fruits and vegetables or stirring.

activities.title: Kitchen helper: tear and spread
activities.summary: At the table, your child tears washed lettuce for a salad and spreads a soft topping thinly with a blunt knife.

notes: Check any food allergies in the family before you start.

items: Blunt butter knife or a spoon

supervision.space: Seated at a table, within your arm's reach, away from the stove, hot pans and sharp knives.

steps: Wash hands together and sit at the table with a bowl and a plate.
Tear the washed lettuce into small pieces for the salad bowl.
Spread a soft topping thinly on bread or crackers with a blunt knife or the back of a spoon.
Serve it at the table and eat it sitting down together.
adaptations: Younger: tearing only, or pressing a cookie cutter into soft bread.
Older: arrange pieces into a face, or count pieces onto each plate.
Allergy in the family: use only foods from their safe list.
stopCues: Eating while walking around: sit back down or pause
Licking the knife or fingers a lot: wash hands

safety.text: For under-4s, avoid or cut up high-risk foods: whole grapes, raw carrot or apple chunks, nuts, popcorn, and thick nut butter (spread it thin).
Eat only sitting down: no running, playing or lying down with food in the mouth.
If anyone has a food allergy, check every label and use clean utensils and surfaces to avoid cross-contact.
Blunt knife or spoon only; keep sharp knives and hot pans out of reach.

why.text: CDC suggests letting preschoolers help prepare healthy foods and then enjoy them together.

activities.title: Plant seeds and water them
activities.summary: Dig a pot or small patch together, press in a few seeds or a seedling, and water it from a small can.

items: A pot, window box or small patch of soil
Seeds such as peas or cress, or a seedling

supervision.space: A garden patch or a pot on a table. No buckets or ponds left with water; chemicals locked away.

steps: Fill a pot or clear a small patch, and let your child dig and break up the soil.
Press a few seeds in a finger-deep, or plant a seedling, and cover them up.
Water gently from a small can or cup, then empty it and put it away.
Wash hands. Check each day together and talk about what has changed.
adaptations: Indoors: grow cress on a damp paper towel on a windowsill.
Older: draw labels for each pot, or measure the plant each week.
No garden: water the houseplants together with a small cup.
stopCues: Soil or seeds going in the mouth

safety.text: Stay beside them while there's water, and empty watering cans and buckets as soon as you've finished.
Keep fertilizer and garden chemicals locked away, and check garden plants are non-toxic.
Seeds are small. Keep packets and spilled seeds away from babies and toddlers.

why.text: HSE suggests a window box or garden patch to dig and grow seeds; AAP says small yard jobs like watering flowers give calming sensory input.

activities.title: Smell the flower, blow the candle
activities.summary: Practise slow breaths together: sniff a pretend flower through the nose, then blow out a pretend candle.

notes: Practise when everyone is calm first; it's easier to use when upset if it's familiar.

supervision.space: Anywhere quiet: the sofa, the floor, or a bench outside.

steps: Hold up a pretend flower and smell it slowly through your nose together.
Then blow out a pretend candle slowly through your mouth.
Do three to five breaths. Lying down, put a soft toy on their tummy and watch it rise and fall.
When they're upset later, invite rather than insist: 'Want to smell the flower with me?'
adaptations: Younger: blow a tissue or a feather to see the breath move.
Older: count 'in, two, three; out, two, three' on your fingers.
Finish with a hug of a favorite toy.
stopCues: Feeling dizzy: go back to normal breathing
Giggly and not into it: try another time
Too upset to try: just stay close

safety.text: Keep breaths slow and gentle, and stop if your child feels dizzy.

why.text: CDC suggests helping 3-year-olds manage stressful feelings by teaching them to take deep breaths, hug a favorite toy, or go to a quiet, safe place.

activities.title: Make a calm-down corner together
activities.summary: Build a cozy corner together with a cushion, a soft toy and books, and name feelings while you set it up.

items: Optional: paper to draw feelings faces

supervision.space: A quiet corner you can see from where you usually are, away from cords and furniture that could tip.

steps: Choose a corner together and add a cushion, a soft toy and two or three books.
Draw simple faces (happy, sad, cross, worried) and name each feeling together.
Practise while calm: go there, hug the toy, take slow breaths.
When they're upset, offer it as a choice, never a punishment, and stay nearby so they can come to you.
adaptations: Younger: just a cushion and a toy, with you sitting there too.
Older: let them choose what goes in and draw their own feelings pictures.
Short on space: a 'calm basket' that goes wherever they are.
stopCues: Treats it as a game: fine, that's still practice
Doesn't want to go: offer a hug instead
Gets more upset alone: stay with them

safety.text: If there's a baby at home, keep loose cushions and blankets out of the baby's play and sleep space.
A calm corner is for comfort with you nearby, never for sending a child away alone.

why.text: CDC suggests creating a spot at home where a child can go when upset, with you nearby, and talking about and naming feelings.
